title: Worsening breathlessness and cough in a 51-year-old retired chef on home oxygen
desc: A focused dyspnoea history and respiratory examination of Nancy Perk, a 51-year-old retired chef with COPD on home oxygen, seen in general practice. Over the past week her breathlessness has worsened and her chronic cough has become more frequent, with foul, purulent sputum and fever, two weeks after she visited her sister in hospital. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, ECG, chest X-ray report, bloods and respiratory virus swab, and diagnoses an infective acute exacerbation of COPD. They exclude the mimics, arrange ambulance transfer with controlled oxygen, bronchodilators, prednisolone and an antibiotic suited to her penicillin allergy, answer her COVID worry and safety-net.
focus: Dyspnoea in known COPD: a history that covers the cardinal exacerbation symptoms, cluster questions for at least six differentials and a COPD examination, then recognising an infective exacerbation, excluding its mimics, and starting safe treatment
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a general practice. Nancy Perk is a 51-year-old retired chef who has come to see her GP because she is short of breath. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first and is in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Ms Perk and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her ECG, her chest X-ray report, and her blood and swab results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Nancy Perk, a 51-year-old retired chef. You are sitting forward in the chair with your portable oxygen cylinder running through nasal prongs. You are breathless: answer in short phrases of 3 to 6 words, stopping for breath, and cough every few minutes (a wet, rattly cough). You feel awful and exhausted, but you are alert and chatty when you can be. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "Hi Doc, I've been feeling awful recently. I've been really short of breath. It is something I struggle with, but I feel it is getting worse."

If asked to say more: "I have had a pretty bad cough as well and it doesn't seem to go away. I'm worried that it is COVID."

The breathlessness (give only when asked):

  • How bad: "It's really terrible. I am needing to use my home oxygen a lot more often." You normally use it overnight and when you get puffed around the house, at 2 litres. This week you have needed it nearly all the time.
  • How far you can go (only if asked about distance or what you can do): "I need oxygen to go from my bed to the living room."
  • Onset and course: it came on gradually over the last week and has slowly got worse. Nothing sudden.
  • Context: 2 weeks ago you visited your sister in hospital. She is having radiotherapy for breast cancer.
  • Better: oxygen and resting. Worse: any activity at all.

The cough (give only when asked):

  • Long-standing: you have had a cough for years. The phlegm is usually pale.
  • Now: "It's keeping me up all day and night." You have coughing fits about every hour, and they are more intense and last longer than usual. You are "knackered" after each one.
  • Sputum: about a teaspoon at a time. It is now yellow, thick and foul-smelling, with white streaks of pus. No blood.
  • Better: clearing the phlegm helps for a bit. Worse: at night. You wake at night coughing, not gasping for breath.
  • Exposures: no recent travel. You might have caught something at the hospital. No dust, asbestos or chemicals at work.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Present: you have felt feverish and hot on and off for a few days. You feel generally unwell, flat and very tired.
  • Absent:
    • No shaking chills or rigors.
    • No sudden onset of breathlessness, and no sharp pain on one side of the chest. Your chest just feels sore from coughing.
    • No coughing up blood.
    • No calf pain or swelling, no long trips and no time stuck in bed (apart from resting this week).
    • No chest pain or tightness on exertion, no sweating, no palpitations or racing heart lately, no fainting.
    • You sleep on 2 pillows, as you always have, and are not more breathless lying flat. No ankle swelling.
    • No weight loss and no night sweats. No asbestos, and no contact with anyone with TB.
    • No asthma as a child, and no hay fever or eczema.

Past medical history:

  • COPD, diagnosed 4 years ago. You have chest physio once a month.
  • A clot on the lung (pulmonary embolus) 2 years ago.
  • An irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation), diagnosed 1 year ago. You haven't felt it lately.
  • High blood pressure for 6 years.
  • Reflux (GORD) for 10 years.
  • If asked about previous flare-ups: "Never this bad. I've never been in hospital for my chest."
  • No cancer, TB or heart attack.

Medications:

  • Ramipril 5 mg once a day.
  • Symbicort (budesonide and formoterol) twice a day.
  • Nexium for the reflux.
  • Vitamin D.
  • Home oxygen, 2 L/min.
  • If asked about a puffer for when you are breathless: "Just the Symbicort, twice a day."
  • If asked about blood thinners: "Not at the moment."

Allergies: penicillin, which gave you a rash.

Vaccinations: up to date, including the pneumonia vaccine and the flu shot every year.

Family history: your mother died of old age at 90. Your father died of a heart attack at 65. You have 2 children, both well.

Social history:

  • Smoking: you smoked 20 cigarettes a day from 15 to 48, then quit when you went on oxygen. You smoked marijuana as a teenager, nothing since.
  • Alcohol: only on special occasions. The last time was Christmas.
  • Work: a chef for 33 years, now retired. You chain-smoked on your breaks.
  • Exercise and diet: you can't exercise. You eat a balanced diet.
  • Home: you live alone. Your children visit weekly. You do your own chores and have your groceries delivered.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are worried you have COVID, because you were at the hospital. You want to know what is wrong and to get your breathing back.

Question to raise: if the candidate has not asked about your worries by the end of the history: "Do you think it's COVID, doctor?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: sitting forward with her hands on her knees (tripod position). Pursed-lip breathing. Speaks in short phrases and uses her neck muscles to breathe. On nasal prongs at 2 L/min from her portable cylinder. Coughs up a small amount of thick yellow sputum during the examination. Alert and oriented. Lips pink, with no central cyanosis.
  • Vital signs (10:10): RR 26/min; SpO2 89% on 2 L/min nasal prongs; HR 108 beats/min, regular; BP 134/82 mmHg; temperature 38.2 °C.
  • Hands: warm. No peripheral or central cyanosis. No clubbing, no tar staining, no tremor. No flapping tremor (asterixis). Pulse 108, regular, not bounding.
  • Neck: trachea central. Reduced cricosternal distance (two finger-breadths) with a tracheal tug. Sternocleidomastoids active. JVP not raised. No lymph nodes.
  • Chest:
    • Inspection: barrel-shaped chest with an increased front-to-back diameter, and indrawing between the ribs.
    • Expansion: reduced but symmetrical.
    • Percussion: hyper-resonant throughout. Cardiac and liver dullness reduced.
    • Auscultation: breath sounds reduced throughout, with a prolonged expiratory phase and widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze. Coarse crackles at both bases change after she coughs. No bronchial breathing, no focal dullness, no pleural rub. Vocal resonance equal on both sides.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds soft but dual, with no murmur. No right ventricular heave.
  • Legs: no ankle or sacral oedema. Calves soft, equal and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms the patient's identity, explains the consultation and gains consent for the history and examination.
Opens with an open question. Recognises that she is breathless and keeps the questions short. Acknowledges her COVID worry, uses plain language and summarises back to her.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:

kids.x: Onset and course: came on gradually over the last week and is slowly getting worse.
Quantifies it by what she can do and her oxygen use: needs oxygen to get from her bed to the living room, and uses her home oxygen much more than usual.
kids.d: A rating out of 10 alone does not earn this item.

kids.x: Relieving and aggravating factors: better with oxygen and rest, worse with any activity.

check.x: Characterises the cough and sputum and compares them with her usual:

kids.x: A cough for years, now with fits about every hour that are more intense and longer than usual. They exhaust her and are worse at night.
Sputum change: usually pale, now yellow, thick and foul-smelling with streaks of pus, about a teaspoon at a time. Asks about blood (none).
Clearing the phlegm helps for a short time.

check.x: Asks about triggers and exposures: visited her sister in hospital 2 weeks ago (a possible sick contact). No recent travel and no occupational exposure.
Asks about systemic symptoms: fever, malaise and fatigue are all present.
Uses cluster questions to screen for the other causes of worsening breathlessness:
check.d: Source marking: full credit for cluster questions covering at least 6 diagnoses, with part credit for 5, 4 or 3. Each diagnosis needs at least one targeted question. Sub-item 2 must be covered.

kids.x: Pneumonia: fever, rigors, pleuritic pain.
Pulmonary embolism: past PE, sudden onset, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, immobility (only the past PE is positive).
Pneumothorax: sudden breathlessness or sharp one-sided chest pain (none).
Heart failure or cor pulmonale: orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling (none).
Arrhythmia or myocardial infarction: palpitations (known AF), exertional chest pain, sweating, syncope (none).
Lung cancer or TB: weight loss, haemoptysis, night sweats, asbestos, TB contact (none).
Asthma: childhood asthma or atopy (none).

check.x: Past medical history: COPD for 4 years on home oxygen with monthly chest physio, PE 2 years ago, AF 1 year ago, hypertension for 6 years, GORD for 10 years. Asks about previous exacerbations or admissions (none this bad, never admitted).
check.d: Critical elements: COPD on home oxygen and the past PE.

check.x: Takes the medication, allergy and vaccination history:

kids.x: Ramipril 5 mg daily, Symbicort twice daily (no reliever), Nexium, vitamin D, home oxygen at 2 L/min. Asks about blood thinners (none at present).
Allergy: penicillin (rash).
Vaccinations up to date, including pneumococcal and annual influenza.

check.x: Family history (not scored): mother died of old age at 90, father died of a heart attack at 65, 2 children well.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking quantified: 20 a day from 15 to 48 (about 33 pack-years), quit when she went on oxygen. Marijuana as a teenager.
Alcohol only on special occasions. Retired chef of 33 years. Unable to exercise. Lives alone with weekly visits from her children, does her own chores and has groceries delivered.
kids.d: Living alone matters for the disposition decision.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations and draws out her worry that this is COVID.
Examination
General inspection for work of breathing: speaking in short phrases, pursed-lip breathing, tripod position, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis (none), oxygen device and flow, and sputum.
Requests a full set of vital signs, including SpO2 with the oxygen flow and temperature. Identifies RR 26, SpO2 89% on 2 L/min, HR 108 regular and temperature 38.2 °C.

Examines the hands and neck: clubbing (none; if present it suggests another cause such as lung cancer or bronchiectasis, because clubbing is not a feature of COPD), asterixis and bounding pulse as signs of CO2 retention (none), tar staining, tracheal position, cricosternal distance and tracheal tug.
Examines the chest front and back and finds the signs of COPD:

kids.x: Inspection and palpation: barrel chest, intercostal indrawing, reduced but symmetrical expansion.
Percussion: hyper-resonant throughout, with reduced cardiac and liver dullness.
Auscultation: reduced breath sounds, prolonged expiration, widespread expiratory wheeze, and coarse basal crackles that change with coughing. No focal bronchial breathing or dullness.

check.x: Looks for heart failure, cor pulmonale and DVT: JVP, heart sounds and right ventricular heave, ankle and sacral oedema, and both calves (all normal).
Interpretation
Observations: febrile, tachycardic and tachypnoeic, with SpO2 88 to 89% on her usual 2 L/min, which falls to 86% after a 20 m walk. States she is not improving and is not safe to manage at home.
ECG: sinus tachycardia with no AF today (compared with the AF on last year's ECG), no ischaemic change and no right heart strain.
Chest X-ray: hyperinflation consistent with COPD, with no consolidation, pneumothorax, effusion or pulmonary oedema.
check.d: Accept in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer. Naming the absent pneumothorax and consolidation is needed.

check.x: Bloods and swab: neutrophilia and CRP 62 fit an infection. Renal function and potassium are normal on ramipril, and Hb is normal (no polycythaemia). SARS-CoV-2, influenza and RSV were not detected.

States the most likely diagnosis: an acute exacerbation of COPD, probably triggered by a respiratory infection. Justifies it with at least four features: known COPD, worsening breathlessness, a sick contact, a more frequent and severe cough, more and purulent sputum, fever, and the relevant negatives.
check.d: Source marking: the diagnosis, plus 0.5 for each justification (maximum 2.5).

check.x: Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against: pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, heart failure, AF.
check.d: Critical element: PE must be one of them, given her past PE and no current anticoagulation. Accept the reasons listed in the ddx.

check.x: Management

Decides with the supervising GP that she needs hospital care today, and arranges ambulance transfer to ED with a phone handover. Gives a reason: she is on home oxygen and needs more, she is febrile and tachypnoeic, she lives alone, and she has comorbidities.
Controlled oxygen: titrates to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92%, avoids high-flow oxygen because of the risk of hypercapnia, and states that she needs a blood gas in hospital.
Starts a short-acting bronchodilator now: salbutamol 4 to 8 puffs (100 micrograms each) via a spacer, repeated as needed. Any nebuliser should be driven by air, not oxygen.
Oral prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days.

Antibiotic for the purulent sputum, chosen for her penicillin allergy: doxycycline 200 mg orally for the first dose, then 100 mg daily, for a total of 5 days (not amoxicillin). Follows up the sputum culture already sent.
check.d: Accept a candidate who starts it in the practice or leaves it to ED, as long as doxycycline is named and amoxicillin is avoided. The sputum culture element is not critical.

check.x: Explains in plain words that this is a flare-up of her COPD brought on by a chest infection, that the COVID test is negative, and why she needs hospital today. Checks understanding.
Safety netting
Gives at least three red flags in plain words: getting more breathless, becoming drowsy, confused or hard to wake, blue lips, new chest pain, coughing up blood, a swollen or painful calf.
Says what to do: while she waits, tell the staff immediately; after discharge, call 000 for these signs.
Arranges follow-up: GP review within 7 days of discharge, a written COPD action plan, a review of her inhalers and technique, and referral to pulmonary rehabilitation.
check.d: Credit at least two of the four. Also accept: considering adding a LAMA (triple therapy) per the COPD-X stepwise approach, reviewing anticoagulation for her AF and past PE, or swapping ramipril if the cough persists.

part2.lead: After your examination the practice nurse recorded an ECG and took a nose swab. The GP arranged an urgent chest X-ray and blood tests at the on-site imaging and pathology service. It is now 11:45 and Nancy is back in the treatment room. Here are her observations, her ECG, her chest X-ray report, and her blood and swab results.
part2.patient:
Nancy is present for question 4. When the candidate explains, she asks, if not already covered:

  • "So it's not COVID?"
  • "Do I really have to go to hospital? Can't you just give me some tablets and let me go home?"
  • "Can someone ring my kids and let them know?"

At first she is reluctant to go to hospital. She accepts once the candidate explains, in plain words, that her oxygen is low even on her usual flow, that she lives alone, and that she needs a blood test for her oxygen and carbon dioxide levels that the practice cannot do.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse, on her own portable oxygen at 2 L/min via nasal prongs (her usual home flow) throughout. The 10:45 set was taken just after she walked about 20 m back from the X-ray room.
handover.model:
Read: at rest, RR 26, SpO2 88 to 89% on 2 L/min, HR 106 to 108 regular, BP 132 to 134/80 to 82, temperature 38.2 then 38.0 °C, alert. After a 20 m walk her RR rose to 30, HR to 118 and SpO2 fell to 86%. No hospital observation chart is used in general practice, so judge these against her COPD target and the clinical picture.

For Nancy: she is febrile, tachycardic and tachypnoeic. At rest she is only at the bottom of her target range (88 to 92%) on her usual oxygen, and she drops below it on minimal exertion. There has been no improvement over 90 minutes. She is alert, with no hypotension, but drowsiness would suggest rising CO2.

What it changes: she is not safe to manage at home. Arrange ambulance transfer to ED, titrate her oxygen to 88 to 92% while she waits, and repeat the observations.

rows.note: On arrival, on her own portable oxygen
Just walked about 20 m back from X-ray; coughing fit; sat down to rest
Seated at rest in the treatment room

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 10:25 today. Nancy Perk, 51.

  • Rate: 108 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia, with a P wave before every QRS. P waves normal in height.
  • Axis: normal (+70°).
  • PR interval: 150 ms.
  • QRS: 92 ms. No bundle branch block. No dominant R wave in V1.
  • QTc: 438 ms.
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression. No T-wave inversion in V1 to V4. No S1Q3T3 pattern.
  • Comparison: the ECG from the practice record 1 year ago showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 96.

Conclusion: sinus tachycardia. No atrial fibrillation today. No ischaemic change and no features of right heart strain.
handover.model:
Read: sinus tachycardia at 108, normal axis, normal PR, QRS and QTc. No ST or T change, and no right axis deviation, RBBB, right precordial T-wave inversion or S1Q3T3.

For Nancy: she is in sinus rhythm, so paroxysmal AF with a fast rate is not driving the breathlessness. The tachycardia fits fever, hypoxaemia and the work of breathing. Having no right heart strain does not exclude PE, but nothing here points to it.

What it changes: a normal QTc is a reassuring baseline before high-dose salbutamol (which can cause hypokalaemia and tachyarrhythmia) and would matter if a macrolide were considered. Her rhythm should be monitored in hospital, as infection and beta-agonists can trigger AF.

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA and lateral, erect, taken at 10:35 today.

Clinical details: 51-year-old woman with COPD on home oxygen. One week of worsening breathlessness, increased purulent sputum and fever 38.2 °C. PE 2 years ago.

Comparison: chest X-ray from 2 years ago.

Technique: not rotated. Adequately exposed. Eight anterior ribs are visible above the right hemidiaphragm in the midclavicular line.

Findings:

  • Lungs: hyperinflated. Peripheral vascular markings are reduced in both upper zones. Mild bronchial wall thickening at both bases, which is new since the previous film. No consolidation, mass or cavity.
  • Pleura: no pneumothorax; lung markings extend to the chest wall at both apices. No pleural effusion.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms flattened. Increased retrosternal air space on the lateral view. Costophrenic angles clear. No free gas.
  • Heart and vessels: narrow, vertical heart with a cardiothoracic ratio of about 0.42. No upper lobe venous diversion, no interstitial or alveolar oedema. Hila normal in size.
  • Airway and mediastinum: trachea central. Mediastinum not widened.
  • Bones and soft tissues: normal.
  • Lines and devices: nasal oxygen tubing only.

Conclusion: hyperinflation consistent with COPD, with mild bibasal bronchial wall thickening. No consolidation, pneumothorax, pleural effusion or pulmonary oedema.
handover.model:
Read: PA and lateral, adequate technique. Hyperinflated lungs (8 anterior ribs), flattened hemidiaphragms and a larger retrosternal air space, with a narrow vertical heart. Bronchial wall thickening at both bases. No consolidation, no pneumothorax (markings reach the chest wall at both apices), no effusion, no oedema or cardiomegaly, and normal hila.

For Nancy: the film shows her COPD and excludes the main mimics that a plain film can show: pneumonia, pneumothorax and an effusion. It makes heart failure unlikely (normal heart size, no oedema). It cannot exclude PE.

What it changes: it supports an exacerbation of COPD. With no consolidation she is treated as an infective exacerbation, not pneumonia. If she fails to improve, or if PE features develop, hospital should consider a CTPA.

handover.label: Blood and swab results
handover.result: Bloods collected at 10:40, urgent; results phoned through at 11:35. No haemolysis. The respiratory PCR was done in the practice on a nasal swab at 10:30. A sputum sample has been sent for microscopy and culture, with the result to follow.
handover.model:
Read: WCC 13.4 with neutrophils 10.6 and CRP 62, which is a neutrophilia with a moderately raised CRP. Hb 151 and platelets are normal. Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and eGFR are normal. SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B and RSV were not detected.

For Nancy: this fits an infective exacerbation, and with the purulent sputum it supports an antibiotic. A normal Hb rules out both secondary polycythaemia and anaemia. Normal potassium and renal function on ramipril give a safe baseline for steroids and salbutamol, both of which can lower potassium. A negative swab answers her COVID worry. A single swab cannot completely exclude COVID or influenza, but it makes them unlikely.

What it changes: start doxycycline (penicillin allergy) and follow the sputum culture. Hospital will add a blood gas, because these bloods cannot measure CO2.

labs.title: Respiratory virus PCR (nasal swab, point of care)

ask: You are now calling the emergency department registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Nancy, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Nancy now, here in general practice.
Nancy asks whether this is COVID and why she has to go to hospital. What would you tell her, what warning signs would you give her, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student at the practice with the supervising GP. Nancy Perk, 51.
  • Situation: probable infective exacerbation of COPD. Sending her by ambulance for ED assessment and likely admission.
  • Background: COPD for 4 years on home oxygen 2 L/min, ex-smoker of 33 pack-years. PE 2 years ago with no current anticoagulation, AF, hypertension on ramipril, GORD. Uses Symbicort. Penicillin allergy (rash). One week of worsening breathlessness, more frequent cough, purulent sputum and fever. Visited hospital 2 weeks ago (possible sick contact).
  • Assessment: T 38.2, HR 108, RR 26, SpO2 89% on 2 L, down to 86% after a 20 m walk. Alert, no asterixis. Wheeze, hyperinflation, basal crackles, no focal signs. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no AF or strain. X-ray: hyperinflation; no consolidation, pneumothorax or oedema. WCC 13.4, CRP 62, UEC normal. COVID, influenza and RSV negative.
  • Recommendation: controlled oxygen 88 to 92%, salbutamol, prednisolone, doxycycline. Please do a blood gas, consider NIV if acidotic, and admit.

Most likely: acute exacerbation of COPD, probably infective. For it: known COPD on home oxygen, a week of worsening breathlessness, a more frequent and severe cough, more and purulent sputum, fever, a hospital sick contact, wheeze and hyperinflation, neutrophilia and CRP 62, and no other cause on the X-ray or ECG.

  • Pulmonary embolism: past PE and not anticoagulated; COPD raises VTE risk. Against: gradual onset with purulent sputum and fever, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or calf signs, no strain on the ECG. CTPA if she is not improving.
  • Pneumonia: fever and raised CRP. Against: no focal signs and no consolidation.
  • Pneumothorax: COPD is a risk factor. Against: gradual onset and none on the X-ray.
  • Heart failure or AF: against: no orthopnoea or oedema, normal JVP and heart size; sinus rhythm.

1. Disposition: discuss with the GP. Ambulance to ED, with a phone handover. She is on home oxygen and needs more, is febrile and tachypnoeic, lives alone and has comorbidities.
  2. Oxygen: titrate to SpO2 88 to 92%. No high-flow oxygen, because of the risk of hypercapnia.
  3. Bronchodilator: salbutamol 4 to 8 puffs via a spacer now, repeated as needed. Ipratropium can be added. Any nebuliser should be driven by air.
  4. Corticosteroid: prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally daily for 5 days.
  5. Antibiotic: purulent sputum and a penicillin allergy, so doxycycline 200 mg first dose, then 100 mg daily for 5 days in total. Follow up the sputum culture already sent.
  6. Expected in hospital: a blood gas, with NIV if there is a hypercapnic acidosis (pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 45). CTPA if PE is suspected.

• Explanation: the COVID test is negative. This is a flare-up of her COPD, brought on by a chest infection. She needs hospital because her oxygen is low even on her usual flow, she needs a blood test for her oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, and she lives alone.
  • Red flags: getting more breathless; drowsy, confused or hard to wake; blue lips; chest pain; coughing up blood; a swollen or painful calf.
  • What to do: tell the staff straight away while she waits. After discharge, call 000.
  • Follow-up: GP review within 7 days of discharge. A written COPD action plan, a review of her inhalers and technique (she has no reliever; consider adding a LAMA), and pulmonary rehabilitation. Review anticoagulation for her AF and past PE.

ddx.dx: Acute exacerbation of COPD, probably infective
ddx.for: Known COPD on home oxygen with a week of worsening breathlessness, a more frequent and severe cough, purulent foul sputum, fever and a hospital sick contact, wheeze and hyperinflation, and neutrophilia with CRP 62.
Previous PE 2 years ago with no current anticoagulation, COPD (raises VTE risk), tachycardia and hypoxaemia.
ddx.against: Gradual onset with purulent sputum and fever, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or calf signs, and no right heart strain on the ECG.

ddx.for: Fever, purulent sputum, neutrophilia and a raised CRP.
ddx.against: No focal dullness or bronchial breathing, and no consolidation on the chest X-ray.

ddx.for: COPD with hyperinflation is a risk factor, and her breathlessness is worse.
ddx.against: Gradual onset with no sharp one-sided pain, symmetrical signs, a changed sputum, and no pneumothorax on the X-ray.

ddx.dx: Acute decompensated heart failure or cor pulmonale
ddx.for: Severe COPD and hypertension, with worsening breathlessness.
ddx.against: No orthopnoea, PND or oedema, JVP not raised, and a small heart with no oedema on the X-ray.

ddx.dx: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate
ddx.for: Known AF and a heart rate of 108.
ddx.against: Regular pulse and sinus tachycardia on the ECG.

guide:
Part 1 is set at about 10:10 in the GP consulting room. Give history details only when asked. Give the distance answer ("bed to the living room") only when the candidate asks about distance or function. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Item 9 follows the source marking: full credit for cluster questions covering at least six diagnoses, with part credit for five, four or three. Each diagnosis needs at least one targeted question. Family history (item 12) is not scored.

The source's examiner question ("What features of COPD might you see on examination?") is marked here through the examination (items 16 to 19). The source lists AF and a past PE but no anticoagulant. If asked, Nancy says she is not on a blood thinner. A candidate who flags this for review earns credit in item 38.

Part 2 is set at 11:45 the same morning. Hand over all four results together and ask the four questions in order. Nancy is present for question 4 and asks her questions if the candidate has not covered them. Credit the X-ray read (item 24) in the ISBAR or in the diagnosis answer, and credit treatment (items 30 to 33) whether it is given in the ISBAR recommendation or the management answer. In practice, bronchodilator therapy and transfer should not wait for results: also credit a candidate who says that in real practice she could have started a bronchodilator and gone to ED straight after the examination, without waiting for results.

A high-performing candidate quantifies the breathlessness by distance and oxygen use, compares the cough and sputum with her usual, finds the fever and the hospital contact, and screens at least six differentials, including PE given her history. They take a careful medication and allergy history and quantify her smoking. They examine for work of breathing, CO2 retention and the chest signs of COPD. In Part 2 they diagnose an infective exacerbation, exclude the mimics from the X-ray and ECG, and send her to hospital on controlled oxygen with a bronchodilator, prednisolone and doxycycline.

A borderline candidate rates the breathlessness out of 10, misses the change in sputum or the past PE, or does not ask about allergies. They then prescribe amoxicillin, give high-flow oxygen, or send a febrile patient on home oxygen home with a review next week.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute exacerbation of COPD, probably infective

An exacerbation of COPD is a clinical diagnosis: an acute, sustained worsening of breathlessness, cough or sputum, beyond the usual day-to-day variation, that needs a change in treatment. Nancy has severe COPD (she is on home oxygen), and over a week she has developed all three cardinal symptoms:

  • worse breathlessness, now needing oxygen to walk from her bed to the living room;
  • a more frequent and severe cough;
  • more sputum, which has become purulent and foul.

She also has a fever and a likely sick contact from her hospital visit. Her nocturnal symptoms and her dependence on oxygen both indicate severe disease. COPD severe enough to need home oxygen by 48 is early: check alpha-1 antitrypsin levels if not already done.

Triggers: about 70% of exacerbations are triggered by respiratory infection, viral or bacterial. The rest relate to environmental pollution or have no identified cause; PE is an important mimic.

Risk factors: severe COPD, previous exacerbations, GORD and pulmonary hypertension.

Taking the history

Quantify breathlessness by what the patient can do and how much oxygen they use, not by a score out of 10. Compare the cough and sputum with the patient's usual: in COPD, a change in sputum colour and volume is the key clue to a bacterial infection. Cluster questions should cover at least six other diagnoses, because several mimic an exacerbation and some are dangerous:

  • pneumonia;
  • PE, with a past PE and no anticoagulation;
  • pneumothorax;
  • heart failure or cor pulmonale (orthopnoea, PND, oedema);
  • arrhythmia (known AF) or myocardial infarction;
  • lung cancer and TB (weight loss, haemoptysis, night sweats, asbestos);
  • asthma and atopy.

Examination findings in COPD

  • Inspection: tachypnoea, pursed-lip breathing, a barrel chest, and a reduced cricosternal distance with a tracheal tug.
  • Percussion: hyper-resonance with reduced cardiac and liver dullness.
  • Auscultation: reduced breath sounds with prolonged expiration, end-expiratory wheeze and coarse crackles.
  • Cyanosis: may be present, particularly in a severe exacerbation. Nancy has none, peripheral or central.
  • Severe exacerbation: accessory muscle use, the tripod position, central cyanosis, severe hypoxaemia, and signs of respiratory failure such as drowsiness, asterixis and a bounding pulse from CO2 retention.
  • Clubbing: not a feature of COPD. If present, look for lung cancer or bronchiectasis.

The results

  • Observations: fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, and saturations at the bottom of her target range on her usual oxygen, falling on minimal exertion.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia, with no AF, ischaemia or right heart strain.
  • Chest X-ray: hyperinflation with no consolidation, pneumothorax, effusion or oedema.
  • Bloods: neutrophilia with a raised CRP; normal Hb, renal function and potassium.
  • Swab: negative for SARS-CoV-2, influenza and RSV.

Together these support an infective exacerbation and argue against the main mimics. Only a blood gas shows hypercapnia or acidosis, which is why patients with severe COPD and worsening hypoxaemia need hospital assessment.

Mimics to exclude

  • Pneumonia: chest X-ray, FBC and CRP.
  • Pneumothorax: COPD is a risk factor. Suspect it with sudden breathlessness, especially if the sputum is unchanged. Look on the X-ray.
  • Pulmonary embolism: COPD raises the risk of PE, and Nancy has had one before. Suspect it when the sputum is unchanged and there is no sign of infection, or when she fails to improve. Assess with Wells, then D-dimer or CTPA.
  • Acute decompensated heart failure: natriuretic peptide, chest X-ray, ECG and echocardiogram.
  • Arrhythmia such as AF: ECG.

Management (COPD-X; eTG Respiratory and Antibiotic)

  • Where to treat: hospital care is indicated for severe underlying COPD (including home oxygen), a marked increase in symptoms or oxygen requirement, significant comorbidities, poor home support, or failure to respond. Nancy has several of these.
  • Controlled oxygen: target SpO2 88 to 92%, avoiding high concentrations that can worsen hypercapnia (TSANZ).
  • Inhaled bronchodilators: salbutamol via a spacer (4 to 8 puffs, repeated as needed) or nebulised. Ipratropium can be added. In hypercapnic patients, drive nebulisers with air, not oxygen.
  • Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally daily for 5 days.
  • Antibiotics: when there is increased sputum purulence or other features of bacterial infection. eTG lists amoxicillin 500 mg orally 8-hourly for 5 days, or doxycycline 200 mg orally for the first dose, then 100 mg daily, for a total of 5 days. Nancy's penicillin allergy makes doxycycline the choice.
  • In hospital: a blood gas. NIV for a hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) despite optimal treatment.

Medicines review

  • Ramipril: ACE inhibitors can cause a dry cough through bradykinin. Other adverse effects include acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia and angioedema. If her chronic cough persists, her antihypertensive could be changed.
  • Beta-blockers: non-selective beta-blockers can cause bronchoconstriction. If her AF needs rate control, a cardioselective agent is preferred.
  • Inhalers: she has no short-acting reliever, and her inhaler therapy and technique need review. She has severe COPD on ICS/LABA alone: consider adding a LAMA (triple therapy) per the COPD-X stepwise approach.
  • Anticoagulation: stroke prevention for her AF and her past PE should be reviewed.

Safety netting and follow-up

Explain that this is a flare-up of her COPD from a chest infection, and that the COVID test is negative. While she waits, she should tell the staff straight away if she becomes more breathless, drowsy or confused, or develops blue lips, chest pain, haemoptysis or a swollen calf. After discharge she should call 000 for any of these.

COPD-X recommends GP follow-up within 7 days of discharge, covering:

  • a written COPD action plan;
  • an inhaler and technique review;
  • pulmonary rehabilitation;
  • vaccinations kept up to date;
  • continued smoking abstinence.
points: An exacerbation of COPD is a clinical diagnosis: a sustained worsening of breathlessness, cough or sputum beyond the usual day-to-day variation. Increased sputum purulence points to a bacterial infection, the trigger in most cases.
Quantify breathlessness by what the patient can do and how much oxygen they need, and compare the cough and sputum with their usual.
Screen at least six differentials with cluster questions. Pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE, heart failure and arrhythmia all mimic an exacerbation, and COPD raises the risk of both pneumothorax and PE.
In COPD, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88 to 92% and drive nebulisers with air. Only a blood gas shows hypercapnia, so a worsening patient on home oxygen needs hospital assessment.

Treat with an inhaled bronchodilator, prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days and, for purulent sputum, an antibiotic. Use doxycycline (200 mg first dose, then 100 mg daily, 5 days in total) if the patient has a penicillin allergy.

After an exacerbation, arrange GP review within 7 days of discharge, a written COPD action plan, an inhaler review and pulmonary rehabilitation. Review medicines such as ACE inhibitors (cough) and non-selective beta-blockers (bronchoconstriction).
